The Strumming Ladder

117 guitar strumming patterns in 10 levels, ordered so that most of them add or remove a stroke or two from a pattern you already know, each with the songs it is heard in and a click track to play along with.

A note from the author. I am not a guitar teacher. I am a student, and I made these materials for my own practice. I am sharing them in case they are useful to someone else, but please do not take them too seriously: I have no experience of teaching anyone but myself. Found a wrong pattern, or a step that feels too big? Tell me here.

The one rule: the hand never stops

Your strumming hand swings like a pendulum, down and up, in time with the count. A pattern is a choice of which swings touch the strings and which pass by in the air.

One bar in each feel. Blue arrows are triplet beats that start on an upstroke; dashed arrows are swings that miss the strings.

The rule in words

Your strumming hand swings like a pendulum, down and up, in time with the count. In quarter-note patterns it goes down on every number and comes back up in between without touching the strings. In eighth-note patterns it goes down on every number and up on every +. In sixteenth-note patterns it goes down on the number and the +, up on the e and the a.

Triplets are the one case where the count does not fix the direction. The count is 1 + a 2 + a, three swings to a beat, and three is odd, so the hand goes down-up-down on beats 1 and 3 and up-down-up on beats 2 and 4. In a shuffle the middle count is left out, and the hand is back to down on the number and up on the a.

How to read the diagrams

↓ Down↑ Up↓ Accent: hit it harder↓• Staccato: cut it short↓ Left-hand mute (dead ‘chk’)↓ Right-hand mute (palm mute or chuck)B Bass string only

Under each diagram the same bar is written in standard rhythm notation, for those who read it. A strum followed by missed counts is written as a longer note, or as tied notes, because the chord keeps ringing. Slash noteheads are strums, x noteheads are muted strums and a round notehead is a bass note. The time signature is left out: a bar has four beats unless the title says 6/8 or 3/4. A swung eighth-note pattern is written in 12/8, the way its diagram counts it; swung sixteenths are written straight.

Listen to a pattern

The click track in words

Press ▶ beside a pattern's title to hear it as a looping click track, at the tempo set in the bar at the top (92 to start with). The tempo counts quarter notes. In 6/8 and 12/8 the eighth note keeps its length, so their beats, which are three eighths long, come at two thirds of the number shown (about 61 a minute at 92). Swing and shuffle patterns keep the beat at the number shown. Two bars of stick clicks count you in first: ‘1, 3’ and then ‘1, 2, 3, 4’ in 4/4 (in 6/8, ‘1, 4’ and then all six; in 3/4, ‘1’ and then ‘1, 2, 3’), and the pattern starts on the next bar. Untick ‘count-in’ to start straight away. Tick ‘guitar’ to hear each pattern strummed on a guitar instead of clicks, on an open G chord and an open C chord a bar each: downstrokes from the low string up, upstrokes on the top four strings, muted strums as a dead ‘chk’. The guitar is made in the browser, so it is close to a real one but not a recording. A bell marks count 1 of every bar that plays something on count 1; a bar that starts with a gap or a note tied over from the bar before gets no bell, so the bell never sounds where you do not strum. Tick ‘bell on 1’ to hear the bell on count 1 of every bar, played or not. A downstroke is a low, round ‘tock’ and an upstroke a short, bright ‘tick’ two octaves higher; an accent is louder; a muted strum is a short ‘chk’ of noise, a palm mute a dull thud, a staccato strum a clipped click and a bass note a low thump. Missed counts are silent unless you turn on ‘tick every beat’, which ticks softly on a beat with no strum and a little louder on a beat that is played. The sounds are made in the browser; there are no audio files. No sound on an iPhone or iPad? Check the volume, and if it is still silent, turn silent mode off.

How to climb

The four steps in words
  1. Rhythm first, no chord. Learn the strumming hand on its own. Rest the fretting hand lightly across all the strings, without pressing, so every strum gives a dead chk and no notes. Strum the pattern like that while counting out loud. Add a chord only when the hand runs by itself.
  2. Slow metronome. 60 bpm for eighth-note patterns, 50–60 bpm for sixteenth-note patterns. Move up about 10 bpm at a time.
  3. One chord, then two. Loop the pattern on one chord for a minute, then over a change such as G to C. The pattern must not hiccup at the change.
  4. Play it with the record. Put on one of the listed songs and strum along – on dead strings, as in step 1, if you do not know the chords. When you can hold the pattern through a whole song, climb to the next one.

Level 1 · Quarter notes

About this level

One strum per beat, or fewer. The job here is a steady hand and clean chord changes - nothing else.

1Half notes: two strums

↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

When We Were Young – Adele (intro) • Sweet Caroline – Neil Diamond (intro) • Sign of the Times – Harry Styles (chorus)

One strum on beat 1, one on beat 3, and let each ring for two beats. Count all four beats out loud. Slow ballads often start like this before the full strum comes in.

2Half notes, then one long strum

↓↓1+2+3+4+
↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

One Call Away – Charlie Puth (intro) • Supermarket Flowers – Ed Sheeran (verse, first two of four bars)

The easiest two-bar pattern: two strums in the first bar, one in the second that rings for all four beats. Keep counting through the long strum.

3Half notes, then a step

↓↓1+2+3+4+
↓↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Let It Go – Idina Menzel (from Frozen; verse, slow)

Two strums per bar, with one extra strum on beat 4 of the second bar to lead back to the start.

4Four on the floor

↓↓↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Say Something – A Great Big World • Jar of Hearts – Christina Perri (chorus)

All downstrokes, one per beat. Let the hand rise silently on each '+' - that silent lift is the upstroke you will add later.

5Quarters with a pickup

↓↓↓↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Comfortably Numb – Pink Floyd • Every Rose Has Its Thorn – Poison

Your first upstroke: a light flick on the '+' of 4 that pushes into the next bar. Later, try hitting just the bass string on beat 2.

Level 2 · Straight eighth notes

About this level

Two slots per beat: '1 + 2 + 3 + 4 +'. Downstrokes land on the numbers, upstrokes on the '+'. The level starts with every slot played and then takes upstrokes away; the all-downstroke and bass-note patterns come after. No upstroke is left hanging over a missing beat yet: that is syncopation, and it starts in level 4.

6Constant down-up aka alternate strumming

↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Sweet Home Alabama – Lynyrd Skynyrd • White Winter Hymnal – Fleet Foxes • Songbird – Oasis • Cheerleader – OMI • Johnny B. Goode – Chuck Berry • Mr. Tambourine Man – Bob Dylan

The hand's natural motion with nothing left out: down on every number, up on every '+'. The eight patterns after it are this one with strokes removed. Accent beats 2 and 4 slightly so it grooves instead of sounding like a machine.

7Constant down-up, then a breather

↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+
↓↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Happier – Ed Sheeran

A full bar of down-up, then a bar of three slow strums on beats 1, 2 and 4. The hand keeps the same motion in both bars; in the second it mostly misses.

8Three upstrokes

↓↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Love Story – Taylor Swift • Last Christmas – Wham! • In My Life – The Beatles • The Man Who Can't Be Moved – The Script

Constant down-up with one stroke removed: the hand misses the strings on the '+' of 1. The long first beat makes the bar breathe.

9Down, down-up

↓↓↑↓↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Let It Be – The Beatles • American Pie – Don McLean • Over My Head (Cable Car) – The Fray • She's Not There – The Zombies

↓↓↑↓↓↑1+2+3+4+
↓↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Many songs repeat a strum every two bars, not every bar. This one is the previous pattern followed by pattern 8. The second bar fills the gap after beat 3, which gives the pair a sense of question and answer.

↓↓↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

↓↓↓↓↑1+2+3+4+

14Down-up on beat 2 only

↓↓↑↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Four downstrokes with a single upstroke after beat 2. A good test of control: the hand must miss the strings on three of its four upswings.

15Driving eighths, all down

↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Free Fallin' – Tom Petty • Chasing Cars – Snow Patrol • Get Back – The Beatles • Yellow – Coldplay • Times Like These – Foo Fighters • Walk on the Wild Side – Lou Reed

Eight downstrokes. This breaks the down/up rule on purpose: the hand has to come back up without touching the strings twice as often, which gives the pumping rock sound. Keep the wrist loose.

16Downstroke drive with gaps

↓↓↓↓↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

I Love Rock 'n' Roll – Joan Jett and the Blackhearts • Highway to Hell – AC/DC

All downstrokes again, but leave the '+' of 2 and the '+' of 4 empty. The gaps are what make the riff punch - classic power-chord rock.

17Boom-chick: bass, strum aka boom-chuck, alternating bass

B↓B↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Hey There Delilah – Plain White T's • I Hear Them All – Old Crow Medicine Show

B = pick only the bass string of the chord (the lowest note you would strum). Bass on 1 and 3, a downstroke on the higher strings on 2 and 4. The simplest country and folk accompaniment.

18Boom-chicka: bass, down-up aka Carter strum, country strum

B↓↑B↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Folsom Prison Blues – Johnny Cash • Ring of Fire – Johnny Cash • Friend of the Devil – Grateful Dead • I Will Follow You Into the Dark – Death Cab for Cutie • New Slang – The Shins

The boom-chick with an upstroke added after each strum. This is pattern 9 with a bass note in place of the first strum - the country and folk sound.

19Bass notes with a run of strums

B↓↑B↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Me and Bobby McGee – Kris Kristofferson • Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) – Eurythmics

Boom-chicka in the first half of the bar; in the second half the bass note is followed by three strums, up-down-up.

20Bass, strum, then a run

B↓↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Take Me Home, Country Roads – John Denver • Blowin' in the Wind – Bob Dylan • Should I Stay or Should I Go – The Clash • Closer to Fine – Indigo Girls • It's the End of the World as We Know It – R.E.M.

One bass note on beat 1, a strum on 2, then straight down-up eighths through beats 3 and 4. A campfire favourite: it sounds full but leaves the first half of the bar open for the singer.

21Strum, bass, strum

↓B↓↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Fix You – Coldplay • The First Cut Is the Deepest – Sheryl Crow • Savin' Me – Nickelback

The bass note moves to beat 2, between two full strums. Gentle and spacious, with one upstroke at the end to lead into the next bar.

22Strum and bass in turns

↓B↓B↓B↓B1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Imagine – John Lennon • Beautiful – Christina Aguilera • Sunshine (Go Away Today) – Jonathan Edwards

Downstroke on every beat, bass note on every '+'. It imitates a piano: chord in the right hand, single notes in the left.

Level 3 · Compound time and waltz

About this level

A change of count, not of difficulty. Until now every beat split into two; in 6/8 it splits into three, and in 3/4 the bar has three beats. Apart from the last pattern, the strumming is even and unsyncopated, so it is no harder than level 2 - it only needs a new way of counting.

23Six-eight: six downstrokes 6/8 time

↓↓↓↓↓↓123456

Hear it in

House of the Rising Sun – The Animals • Until I Found You – Stephen Sanchez (chorus)

Compound time: two beats per bar, each made of three. Six downstrokes, leaning on 1 and 4. Count 'ONE two three FOUR five six'.

24Six-eight with gaps 6/8 time

↓↓↓↓123456

Hear it in

Perfect – Ed Sheeran (chorus) • Until I Found You – Stephen Sanchez (verse)

Leave out counts 2 and 5. Each half of the bar becomes long-short: the lilting ballad feel.

25Six-eight with upstrokes 6/8 time

↓↓↑↓↑123456

Hear it in

Hallelujah – Jeff Buckley • All I Want – Kodaline

The hand alternates down-up on the six counts. Miss count 2, play everything else. A common strummed 6/8 pattern.

26Waltz strum (3/4) 3/4 time

↓↓↑↓↑1+2+3+

Hear it in

Norwegian Wood – The Beatles • Annie's Song – John Denver • Iris – Goo Goo Dolls • Nothingman – Pearl Jam

Three beats per bar, each split in two - simple time, not compound, but it sits here because the bar counts in three. Down on 1, then down-up, down-up.

27Waltz with a push, then the waltz strum 3/4 time

↓↑↑1+2+3+
↓↓↑↓↑1+2+3+

Hear it in

Riverwide – Sheryl Crow

The only two-bar pattern in three found in the song data, and harder than the rest of this level: bar 1 strums beat 1 and then only the '+' of 2 and of 3, so beats 2 and 3 are skipped. Bar 2 is the plain waltz strum. Come back to it after level 4 if the skipped beats throw you.

Level 4 · Syncopated eighth notes

About this level

Syncopation starts when you skip a downstroke ON a beat: the hand still goes down, but misses the strings. An upstroke with no downstroke after it is the sound of syncopation.

↓↑↓↑↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Constant down-up, but the hand ghosts past the strings on beat 3. Say '3' out loud while you miss it.

35The long pause

↓↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

36One push

↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Sweet Child O' Mine – Guns N' Roses (acoustic arrangement) • Don't Stop Believin' – Journey (chorus)

Just two strums: down on 1, then an upstroke on the '+' of 2 that rings across beats 3 and 4. Keep the hand swinging through the silence so the next bar starts in time.

37Push and answer

↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Is She Really Going Out with Him? – Joe Jackson

The push from the previous pattern, answered by a down-up on beat 4. The strums fall in a 3 + 3 + 2 grouping - the tresillo, which the next pattern makes with accents instead of gaps.

38Tresillo accents aka 3 + 3 + 2, the 'Clocks' rhythm

↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Clocks – Coldplay • Glycerine – Bush • Downtown Train – Tom Waits

Eight even downstrokes, but lean hard on 1, the '+' of 2, and 4. The accents group the eighths 3 + 3 + 2 - the tresillo, a rhythm that came into pop from Cuban music. The hand plays straight; only the accents are syncopated.

39The Bo Diddley beat aka based on the 3-2 clave, hambone

↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+
↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Bo Diddley – Bo Diddley • Not Fade Away – The Rolling Stones • I Want Candy – The Strangeloves • Magic Bus – The Who • (Marie's the Name) His Latest Flame – Elvis Presley

Bar 1 is pattern 38 played down-up: 1, the '+' of 2, and 4. Bar 2 answers with two accents, on 2 and 3. Keep the down-up going lightly and hit the five accents hard; say 'bomp, ba-bomp-bomp ... bomp, bomp'. Many players mute the light strokes with the fretting hand so only the accents ring. The tempo is fast, but the count is eighth notes, as Bo Diddley plays it; over a halftime drum feel the same rhythm is counted as one bar of sixteenths.

40Clave from the other side aka 2-3 clave

↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+
↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Practice pattern 39 and this one back to back, four bars each, without stopping

The previous pattern with its two bars swapped: first the two accents on 2 and 3, then the three-accent bar. In Cuban music and salsa the melody decides which bar comes first, and it stays that way for the whole song; musicians call a song '3-2' or '2-3'. Learn both, so you can come in on either side.

Level 5 · Triplets and shuffle

About this level

Three even strums per beat: count '1 + a 2 + a 3 + a 4 + a'. The patterns start with every count played, first all downstrokes and then alternating, and thin them out a strum or two at a time. Then the middle count of every beat is left out. That gap is the shuffle, or swing: the long-short feel of blues, rock and roll and a great deal of folk. The shuffle patterns thin out the same way. Almost every beat is still played (one two-bar pattern stops a beat early), so syncopation waits for the next level.

50Triplets, all downstrokes 12/8 time

↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓1+a2+a3+a4+a

Hear it in

You Are the Reason – Calum Scott (intro and verse) • Everybody Hurts – R.E.M.

Start here: twelve even downstrokes, leaning on the first of each three. Only practical at slow tempos, which is exactly where it is used: slow ballads.

Level 6 · Syncopated triplets

About this level

The syncopated-eighth patterns of level 4, played with the triplet feel. A beat is skipped and the upstroke before it - now on the late 'a' of the triplet - hangs over the gap. If level 4 is solid, the hand already knows these; only the timing is new. The first pattern alternates a plain shuffle bar with a bar that misses beat 3, and the next two patterns each take one more strum away. The patterns after those are versions of the last of them: two-bar forms, a longer pause, a bass note and a tie across the bar line.

Practice pattern – one missing strum, with a plain bar to recover in

One bar of the plain shuffle, then the same bar with the downstroke on beat 3 left out. The hand still moves down on beat 3; it only misses the strings. Loop the two bars until the gap stops pulling you off the beat.

Level 7 · Muting: left hand and right hand

About this level

Silence and 'chk' sounds are part of the rhythm. The left (fretting) hand mutes by letting go; the right (strumming) hand mutes by touching the strings. Same eighth-note motion as before - only the sound changes.

78Left-hand mute: ring, then choke

↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Practice pattern – the basis of every percussive strum that follows

Left hand. Play two beats ringing, then release the pressure of the chord without lifting off - fingers stay touching, slightly flattened - and strum two beats of dead 'chk'. No pitch should sound. Squeeze again on beat 1.

79Strum and scratch

↓↑↓↑↓↑↓↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Practice pattern – the left-hand mute on every second beat

Left hand. One beat of chord, one beat of scratch. The fretting hand pumps: squeeze, release, squeeze, release. Keep the strumming hand moving evenly; only the fretting hand changes the sound.

80Staccato: strum and cut

↓↓↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Practice pattern – the same cut is used on the off-beats in the next pattern

Staccato means short. Strum, then kill the chord straight away so each strum is a clipped 'chop' with silence after it. With fretted chords, relax the left hand right after the strum (as in pattern 78, but after the chord has sounded). With open chords, drop the side of the right hand onto the strings instead.

↑↑↑↑1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

The reggae and ska 'skank': every beat is skipped and only the '+'s sound, each one cut short. Tap your foot on the beats or you will drift onto them.

↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓1+2+3+4+

Hear it in

Smoke on the Water – Deep Purple • Beds are Burning – Midnight Oil • Hot N Cold – Katy Perry • 1985 – Bowling for Soup

Right hand. Rest the edge of the palm on the strings exactly where they leave the bridge and play all downstrokes. You should still hear the notes, but tight and thuddy. Too far from the bridge and the note dies. Lift the palm for the chorus to open the sound up.

Level 8 · Straight sixteenth notes

About this level

Four slots per beat: '1 e + a'. The hand now moves twice as fast: down on the number and the '+', up on 'e' and 'a'. The level starts with all sixteen strokes and takes them away a few at a time, first the 'e's, then the 'a's, then the '+'s. Start at 60 bpm.

In the style of Jimmy Nolen's guitar with James Brown, not a transcription. Hit the chord hard and short on 1 (the One), then keep all sixteen strokes going as left-hand-muted scratches. The chord sounds only in three short stabs off the beat: the 'a' of 2, the '+' of 3 and the 'e' of 4. Use a small ninth-chord shape (E9) on the top strings, and let go of it the moment it sounds.

Every beat starts with a muted down-up - a chuck on the beat, then a dead upstroke with the fretting hand relaxed - and ends with a ringing down-up, all swung. The strumming hand never stops; the fretting hand squeezes and releases once per beat.

About the songs

A strumming pattern is a player's reading of a recording, not a fixed fact: players vary the strum from bar to bar, sections differ, and lessons often simplify. Some pairings are a player's strummed arrangement of a song that has no strummed guitar on the record. The song pairings come from guitar-lesson and tab sites and were not checked against the recordings. Treat each song as a place where the pattern fits and can be heard, then let your ear refine it.

The Fingerpicking Ladder

77 fingerpicking patterns in 10 levels, from a steady thumb to Travis picking, percussion and tremolo. Most add, move or remove one or two notes of a pattern you already know. Press ▶ to hear a pattern played on its chord, at the tempo set in the bar at the top.

New. The patterns come from guitar lessons, tabs and Giuliani’s 120 right-hand studies; the song pairings are weaker than the patterns, and each says when it is an arrangement rather than the record, or when the record is played with a pick. Found a wrong pattern, or a step that feels too big? Tell me here.

Two rules

The two rules in words

The thumb keeps the time. In almost every pattern the thumb plays on the beat and never stops; finger notes come and go around it. Learn the thumb part alone first.

The fingers own strings. Index on string 3, middle on 2, ring on 1. When the chord changes, only the thumb moves to another string. A few patterns move the fingers, and the diagram shows it.

How to read the diagrams

Reading the diagrams in words

Each row is a string, string 1 (the thinnest) at the top, as in tab. Each column is a count. A letter in a circle says which finger plucks that string on that count; two or more circles in one column are plucked together. The buttons under the title mark the chord the pattern is drawn on.

p Thumbi Indexm Middlea Ringp Thumb, palm-muted↓ Index brushes down↑ Index brushes uph Hammer-on (fretting hand)× Slap the strings

p, i, m and a are the Spanish names of the fingers, used in most books.

How to climb

The five steps in words
  1. Thumb alone. Play only the thumb part on one chord, counting out loud, until you could hold a conversation while it runs.
  2. Add one finger note at a time. Open strings or one easy chord first.
  3. Slow click. Loop the pattern with the click track. One teacher says 60 or slower with one pluck per click: for an eighth-note pattern that is 30 on the slider, which counts quarter notes.
  4. Change chords without stopping the thumb. First between chords whose root is on the same string, then between different strings. The chord buttons under each pattern’s title move it to open strings or to C, A, G, E or D, and redraw it: the thumb moves to that chord’s bass strings and the fingers keep theirs (on D, a finger that would share string 3 with the thumb moves up a string). The marked button is the chord the pattern is drawn on. Patterns that change chord themselves, use drop D, or need a note below an open string keep their own.
  5. Then songs. When you know two or three patterns, mix them in one practice session.

Level 2 · Rolls in three

One finger for each string: index on 3, middle on 2, ring on 1. The thumb starts each group and the fingers roll up and back. Courses disagree on the first pattern to teach; many start with these rolls. Mauro Giuliani's 120 right-hand studies (1812, public domain, free on IMSLP) drill figures like these over one C-G7 change, varying only the right hand. Patterns of this ladder that share a figure with one of them, or are taken from one, name the study under the tip.

Practice pattern – Giuliani's right-hand study No. 52

Level 9 · Slap, brush and strum-pick

Percussion and two-finger playing: the hand hits the strings like a snare drum on 2 and 4, or the index brushes chords between the thumb's notes.

The fretting hand joins the pattern, and the patterns become styles. Beyond this are whole solo pieces.
